Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: Last weekend, I decided to celebrate my friend's birthday, and I drank quite a bit of whiskey—about five shots in just a few hours. The next day, I woke up feeling euphoric and overly energetic, which was unusual for me. I was chatting with everyone and couldn’t seem to sit still, even though I later realized it was likely just the hangover giving me that high.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I often find myself feeling upbeat and cheerful, but it usually comes in waves rather than being a constant state. For instance, during a recent family gathering, I felt particularly happy and engaged, laughing and sharing stories, but I never thought it was anything more significant than just enjoying the moment with my loved ones. It doesn't really interfere with my daily life or responsibilities, so I haven’t felt the need to discuss it further.

Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication
Patient_Story: After that birthday celebration, I felt like I was on top of the world, but the next day took a turn. I woke up with a pounding headache and felt a deep sense of anxiety that I couldn't shake off. It lasted for hours, making it hard for me to focus on anything, and I found myself pacing around the apartment, feeling restless and irritable. I realized that I was experiencing a withdrawal from the alcohol I had consumed, which was unsettling for me since I'd never felt this way before.

Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced mood swings that seem to be a result of any substances or medications. In fact, I don’t really take any medication regularly and only drink socially, like at my friend's birthday party. I usually stick to one or two drinks, and I don't find that it affects my mood in any lasting way beyond what I mentioned after that night.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I've never had any significant health issues that would affect my mood. I do visit my doctor for routine check-ups, and I've been told I'm generally in good health. I feel like the ups and downs I experience regarding my mood are more due to life's events, like spending quality time with friends or dealing with stress from work, rather than any medical condition.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I’ve noticed that my memory has been pretty sharp lately. For instance, just last week, I was able to recall specific details from a conversation I had with a colleague months ago about a project we worked on together. Even when I’m multitasking at work, I can keep track of multiple tasks without feeling overwhelmed. It doesn’t seem to impact my day-to-day functioning at all, so I’m not really concerned about any cognitive decline.

Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any significant cognitive issues or behavioral disturbances due to a medical condition. For example, I’ve been managing a mild asthma condition for years, but it only acts up during heavy exercise or when I’m exposed to allergens. Overall, it doesn’t affect my everyday life or lead to any behavioral changes; I just carry an inhaler and make sure to avoid triggers.

Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition
Patient_Story: I don't have any underlying medical conditions that would cause mood disorders. I’ve been pretty healthy overall, and my doctor has always confirmed that I’m in good shape during my routine check-ups. While I do experience some fluctuations in my mood from time to time, I believe they stem from everyday life stresses rather than any medical issues.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: During the past month, I had a couple of days where I felt unusually happy, like the time I went hiking with friends and couldn't stop smiling and joking around. However, these moments were brief and didn't last longer than a few hours, and I didn't have any significant changes in my energy or activity levels afterward. Overall, my mood has been stable, and I haven't experienced a long-term elevated or irritable mood, so I'm not sure if there's anything to be concerned about.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences that felt like delusions or hallucinations. For example, I went to a concert last month and was completely immersed in the music and the atmosphere, but I never felt like I saw or heard things that weren’t there. Everything felt real and grounded; I was just enjoying the moment with my friends. Overall, my perceptions have always seemed clear to me.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I've had moments where I've felt a little off, but I can’t really recall any psychotic symptoms. The other day, I was sitting on my couch watching TV, and I got really caught up in the plot, but I never felt confused about reality or thought anything unusual was happening. My mood was just a bit low, but it wasn’t tied to any kind of manic or depressive episode—it was just a day like any other.

Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: During my recent family trip, I did have a couple of days where I felt extremely happy and energized, almost euphoric while we were hiking and sharing stories around the campfire. However, those feelings were fleeting and quickly returned to my usual baseline, without any accompanying irritability or delusions. I can confidently say that I've never had any experiences that felt like psychosis or significant mood disruptions, and my overall emotional state has been pretty stable.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had any experiences that suggest a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. Just last week, while discussing a project with my colleagues at work, I felt completely present and engaged, without any confusion or unusual thoughts. Everything made sense, and I was able to express my ideas clearly, which reassured me that my mind is functioning well.

I noticed moments of exhilaration, especially when we reached a beautiful viewpoint, but these feelings faded quickly, and I returned to my typical mood without any erratic shifts. Overall, I believe my emotions reflect life's ups and downs rather than any underlying disorder, as my mood has been consistent and stable.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I've had periods where I felt really uplifted, like when I went out to watch a comedy show with friends last month and couldn't stop laughing. I was in a great mood for a few hours, but it didn’t last long; I returned to my usual self afterward and didn't experience any irritability or changes in energy that would concern me. As for depression, I've had days when I felt a bit down, but they were always associated with specific events, like stress at work, and never felt like a major depressive episode.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any delusions or hallucinations in my life. For instance, just last week, I was out with friends at a lively restaurant, enjoying our meals and laughter, and I felt completely grounded in reality. Everything was clear, and I was fully aware of what was happening around me, which reassures me that my thoughts and perceptions are stable.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I can't say I've experienced any psychotic symptoms during depressive episodes, as I don't recall ever having a major depressive episode in the first place. For example, last month, I had a few days where I felt a bit low due to work stress, but I was still able to function and didn't have any unusual thoughts or experiences. My mood returned to normal after addressing the stressor, and I felt clear-headed throughout, without any signs of psychosis.

Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: During a recent weekend trip, I felt an overwhelming sense of joy while hiking with my friends, and I found myself laughing and enjoying the moment. However, I realized that these feelings were fleeting and completely tied to the enjoyable experience of being outdoors with people I care about. I don't experience any psychotic symptoms, and my mood tends to fluctuate based on normal life events rather than any underlying disorder.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any symptoms of a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. Last Saturday, I attended a friend's wedding and was fully engaged with everyone around me, sharing laughs and heartfelt conversations. There were moments of joy and excitement, but I remained clear-headed throughout the event, without any feelings of confusion or unusual thoughts; everything felt completely normal and grounded.

Description: Bipolar II disorder
Patient_Story: Though I've had moments of feeling really upbeat, like when I went out for a friend's birthday and was genuinely enjoying myself, I’ve never experienced prolonged mood swings or drastic shifts in my emotional state. For instance, the day after my friend's celebration, I felt a bit anxious, but it was due to a hangover rather than any underlying mood disorder. Overall, my emotions tend to be stable and are mostly influenced by day-to-day experiences rather than any significant mood episodes.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced prolonged periods of hypomanic symptoms lasting two years or more. For example, while I do have days where I feel particularly energetic or happy, like during a recent beach day with friends where I was playful and lively, these feelings are short-lived and associated with the specific occasion. Overall, my mood has been fairly stable, and I wouldn’t describe it as anything beyond the normal ups and downs of life.

Description: Cyclothymic
Patient_Story: I’ve never had prolonged hypomanic episodes. For instance, last month I had a fantastic day at the beach with friends where I felt really energetic and playful, but it was just a one-off joyful experience rather than a consistent state. After that day, my mood returned to its usual level, and I haven't noticed any long-lasting shifts in my emotions or behavior since then.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: Last week, I went to the casino with some friends, and while I felt an adrenaline rush and a thrill from playing the slots, it was really just part of the fun of the night. I didn't feel euphoric or on top of the world; my mood stayed pretty much the same throughout the evening. I didn't find myself trapped in that high feeling like some people do; once we left, I returned to my normal self without any lingering excitement.

I spent a few late nights organizing my tasks and communicating with my team, and despite the stress, I felt a sense of accomplishment once everything was completed. I didn’t realize any significant distress from the situation; in fact, I felt more resilient afterwards, so I don't think my response was maladaptive at all.

Patient_Story: I can't say I've ever experienced the symptoms associated with bipolar disorder. For example, I've had days where I felt particularly cheerful after a fun outing with friends, but those feelings were always short-lived and tied to specific events in my life. Overall, my mood tends to be stable, and I haven’t noticed any significant fluctuations or episodes that would make me think I have a mood disorder.

Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood
Patient_Story: While I've had fleeting moments of happiness, like when I went to a concert with friends and felt really good during the performance, it was never anything that lasted beyond the night. The next day, I went back to my usual self and didn’t notice any sustained feelings of elevated mood. Overall, my emotional state tends to remain steady, and I don’t think I experience any abnormalities in my mood.

Description: Healthy
Patient_Story: I often feel like I'm in good health overall. Just the other day, I went for my routine check-up, and my doctor confirmed that my blood pressure and cholesterol levels are normal. I take care to eat well and exercise regularly, so I don't believe I have any underlying medical conditions that could be affecting my mood or mental state.
